items.text: Masking debt doesn't work like tiredness. It compounds like interest — invisible until it isn't. The crash that felt sudden has been building for years.
items.rationale: The debt/interest metaphor makes a confusing timeline legible. It explains the 'I was fine and then suddenly I wasn't' pattern without self-blame — a moment of recognition for many late-diagnosed autistic adults.

items.text: Rest doesn't cure autistic burnout if the conditions that caused it haven't changed. You're not failing to recover. You're recovering into the same situation.
items.rationale: Directly challenges the 'just rest' advice most autistic people actually receive. Reframes stalled recovery as a structural problem rather than a personal failing — which is both truer and kinder.

items.text: AuDHD: you build the most detailed plan you've ever written. Then your brain refuses to start it. That's not laziness or failure. It's two incompatible operating modes living in one body.
items.rationale: Names a highly specific, recognizable AuDHD experience backed by community-scale survey data. The 'two incompatible operating modes' framing converts a common self-criticism into a neurological explanation.

items.text: For many neurodivergent workers, remote work wasn't a flexibility perk. It was the accommodation making the job doable. RTO mandates removed it — without calling it what it was.
items.rationale: Shifts the frame from 'neurodivergent people are struggling' to 'a working accommodation was quietly revoked.' Names who holds accountability without telling anyone how to feel about it.

items.text: Late autism diagnosis: relief is real. So is grief — for the years, the misread, the self-blame. Nobody tells you that anger and confusion are equally normal. Rushing past the grief often backfires.
items.rationale: Addresses a genuine gap in late-diagnosis content. The internet skews heavily toward gratitude narratives; naming grief as valid fills something quietly missing for a large and growing cohort.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't permissive parenting. It's structure designed around capacity rather than compliance. Conflating the two compounds shame for families already under enormous pressure.
items.rationale: Provides specific, usable language to distinguish the two approaches. Validates PDA families without attacking those who misread the approach — treats it as a category error, not malice.

items.text: PDA demand avoidance isn't defiance or manipulation. It's a nervous system registering perceived loss of autonomy as a threat. The child isn't choosing this — which is why consequence-based approaches don't reach it.
items.rationale: Compassionate to child and parent simultaneously: removes blame from the child while explaining why well-intentioned conventional approaches fail, without condemning parents for having tried them.
items.sensitivity_flag: The claim that consequence-based approaches categorically 'don't reach it' is strong. Defensible within PDA literature but could read as absolute — may draw pushback from practitioners using blended models.

items.text: Mask and burn out, or disclose and risk your career. That's the bind neurodivergent workers describe. The question isn't 'should I disclose?' — it's why those are still the only two options.
items.rationale: Asks the structural question rather than the personal one. Opens genuine discussion without prescribing an answer — which is more honest and more likely to generate meaningful conversation than a tips thread.

items.text: 'Unmask' has become a rallying word in neurodivergent spaces. For many, that's genuinely freeing. For some, unmasking isn't safe or possible right now. The push to unmask can quietly become its own demand.
items.rationale: Protects people who can't yet safely unmask from new community pressure while honoring the broader unmasking conversation. Models the kind of nuance this community values and rarely sees modeled publicly.

items.text: If you're AuDHD and you make detailed plans you can't start: that gap isn't a character flaw. It's a recognized neurological mismatch. Naming it correctly changes what kind of help makes sense.
items.rationale: Moves the AuDHD planning-initiation validation toward action — naming the experience accurately is itself a step toward actually useful support. Ends with direction without prescribing a specific intervention.

items.text: Autistic burnout recovery means looking at what created the burnout — the demands, the masking requirements, the inaccessible environments. Rest is part of it. Removing the cause is the other part.
items.rationale: Moves the burnout reframe into actionable territory without being prescriptive. The parallel final sentences keep it memorable and give people something concrete to hold onto rather than just a critique of 'just rest' advice.

items.text: If your company issued an RTO mandate, did anyone discuss it as an accessibility decision? For many neurodivergent workers, it was — just one made without them.
items.rationale: Short and pointed. Asks whether neurodivergent workers were at the table when RTO decisions were made — reframes the accommodation question from individual hardship to collective decision-making, which is a sharper and more accurate frame.
